newsitem.title: USA: U.S. study says surgical gloves let viruses through.
newsitem.headline: U.S. study says surgical gloves let viruses through.

text.p: Deadly infections that thousands of patients contract during a hospital stay could be spreading through the very barrier that is supposed to block them -- the surgeon's latex gloves, according to a new study.

Medical Device Technologies, a San Diego company that makes electronic monitoring devices for latex gloves, said on Thursday it tested 11 different brands of gloves in three separate studies and found all the brands failed at one time or another in simulated surgical conditions.

The company said that some of the gloves tested failed "right out of the box," while others showed a propensity to leak later during surgery after they had become saturated with fluid. It did not provide specific data comparing different brands of gloves, but said that of the gloves tested, 21 percent that had passed U.S. Food and Drug Administration test methods were found to allow small numbers of viruses to seep through.

While earlier studies have shown infections spread when gloves are torn or punctured, the latest test suggested many more gloves believed to be intact could also be failing to provide a barrier because of the porous quality of the latex.

U.S. Centres for Disease Control and Prevention data shows that about 2 million patients a year in the United States become infected during a hospital stay, and that about 77,000 of them die from infection. The data does not break down the different ways infections are spread.
The FDA-mandated test for surgical gloves involves filling them with water and hanging them upside down. If the glove leaks within two minutes, it fails the test.
An FDA spokeswoman said on Thursday the agency "would be happy" to look at the study by Medical Device Technologies, but could not comment on the results until it had done so.
